open_obligations: Check whether both studies use comparable hard QuALITY subsets, and whether the two-turn study reuses the single-turn arguments
Note that judges differ (Upwork judges with a 5-minute limit here vs MTurk judges with 90 seconds of passage access in the single-turn study)
Confirm the baselines match: the two-turn study compares PSA with PS only, without the passage-only condition

Note that the two-turn judges had abstention incentives: when abstaining was only minimally incentivized, accuracy got slightly worse with (counter-)arguments, and when judges were incentivized to abstain unless very confident there was no effect; the cited single-turn passage describes no abstention option.
out.other_title: Single debate-style arguments were not found to improve human accuracy in the authors' long-context multiple-choice QA set-up
out.rationale: The authors explicitly describe their two-turn null result as mirroring Parrish et al.'s single-turn null result, so the findings agree.
out.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Whether debate-style arguments help human judges on hard reading comprehension; holds for one or two turns of human-written arguments

text: The authors state that, mirroring the mostly null results of Parrish et al. (2022), adding counter-arguments does not improve human crowdworkers' accuracy on hard multiple-choice reading comprehension questions with time-limited passage access, compared with an argument-free baseline. With weak abstention incentives accuracy gets slightly worse, and with strong incentives there is no effect.
title: Two-turn counter-arguments also fail to help, mirroring Parrish et al.'s mostly null results
